those who know the state or word characterized by that emptiness

items.question: What consequence follows for knowers of the state empty of all views and knowledge?
premises: There are knowers of a state devoid of all views and knowledge.
This state is being considered as a possible locus of description.
items.inference: The implications for such knowers must be examined in the following argument.

rows.grounds: paśyantī, the intermediate level of speech
state of being described or characterized
locative example of a graspable object
identity with the object to be grasped
undesired consequence in a reductio argument

items.question: Would describing paśyantī speech entail its oneness with a graspable object like the hand?
premises: Paśyantī speech may be taken as being described.
The hand is an example of a graspable object.
If described as graspable, identity with the graspable would follow.
items.inference: Describing paśyantī in that way would wrongly make it one with a graspable object.
items.plain_english: If paśyantī were described in that way, it would collapse into oneness with a graspable object like the hand.

rows.grounds: instrumental referring to the object grasped by it

items.question: Would identity with its graspable object wrongly result in the organ of action?
premises: An organ of action relates to a graspable object.
If speech were treated as graspable, identity could be extended.
Such identity would entail oneness with that object.
items.inference: Oneness with the graspable object would wrongly result in the organ of action.
items.plain_english: Then oneness with that graspable object would wrongly result in the organ of action.

rows.grounds: that object as something to be seen or observed
the reflective awareness taking the form 'that is to be seen'

items.question: Does reflective awareness of an object as to be seen arise prior to action?
premises: Action involves an object taken as to be seen or grasped.
Reflective awareness can precede overt action.
Such awareness would have the form 'that is to be seen'.
items.inference: A prior reflective awareness of the object as to be seen would arise.
items.plain_english: Before that, there would be the reflective awareness: 'that is to be seen.'

rows.grounds: taking the form of desire or will

items.question: Is reflective awareness likewise established here in the form of will?
premises: Reflective awareness precedes the manifestation of action.
Will is a form of that reflective awareness.
The same structure applies in the present case.
items.inference: Reflective awareness is likewise established here in the form of will.
items.plain_english: Likewise, reflective awareness is established here also in the form of will.

rows.grounds: wave or stirring forth of consciousness
turned toward or ready for action

items.question: What condition holds before consciousness assumes a subtle manifestation facing action?
premises: Consciousness can manifest in a subtle form.
That manifestation can be oriented toward action.
A prior state exists before such orientation is established.
items.inference: The argument considers the state before consciousness stands as a subtle action-facing manifestation.
items.plain_english: As long as the subtle manifestation of consciousness, facing action, has not yet arisen,

rows.grounds: the process of worldly becoming or manifestation
even subtler than the previously mentioned state

items.question: Does the process of becoming also rest on an even more subtle state?
premises: The process of becoming unfolds in stages.
Subtle manifestations of consciousness precede action.
An even subtler ground can be posited prior to that process.
items.inference: Thus, in the process of becoming also, there is an even more subtle state.
items.plain_english: Thus, in the process of becoming as well, there is an even more subtle state.

rows.grounds: the state of having the nature of Brahman
of a pot and similar objects
imperative inviting the statement or admission

items.question: Should the nature of Brahman be admitted even for objects like a pot?
premises: A subtle state underlies the process of becoming.
If that ground is ultimate, it may extend to all things.
Objects like a pot are included in all things.
items.inference: The Brahman-nature of even a pot and the like should be stated or admitted.
uncertainties: brahmarūpatva may be used provisionally before the shift to śivātmatā.
items.plain_english: Let it be stated that even a pot and the like have the nature of Brahman.

rows.grounds: of a pot and similar objects

items.question: Can the same ultimate nature be affirmed in this way for a pot and similar objects?
premises: The previous verse proposed admitting Brahman-nature for a pot.
The argument seeks consistency across all objects.
The same reasoning applies to pot and the like.
items.inference: Thus, let the same be stated for a pot and similar objects.
items.plain_english: Thus, let the same be said of a pot and the like.

rows.grounds: even of the organ of speech
on the other hand or further

items.question: Is the supreme state absent when considered merely as the organ of speech?
premises: The organ of speech can be considered as an instrument.
The supreme state transcends instrumental limitation.
Likewise comparison extends the argument to speech.
items.inference: Likewise, that supreme state does not belong to the organ of speech as such.
items.plain_english: Likewise, that supreme state does not belong to the organ of speech either.

rows.grounds: means or organ functioning as instrument
of the word or sound having nāda and related forms
identity with or nature of Śiva

items.question: Can an instrument of sound-formed speech possess the nature of Śiva as instrument?
premises: Speech can function as an instrument producing sound-forms.
An instrument is limited by its function.
The question concerns whether Śiva-nature belongs to it qua instrument.
items.inference: The instrument of sound-formed speech does not have Śiva-nature as an instrument.
uncertainties: The syntax is compressed; the verse contrasts instrumentality with Śiva-nature.
items.plain_english: As an instrument of sound-formed speech, it does not have the nature of Śiva.

rows.grounds: by means of speech or voice

items.question: Why must all things be affirmed as having the nature of Śiva despite instrumental limits?
premises: Śiva-nature is not admitted in speech merely as an instrument.
The limitation belongs to the instrumental form, not the ultimate ground.
The same ground underlies all manifestations.
items.inference: Therefore, all is of the nature of Śiva.
items.plain_english: It is not accepted as such through speech as an instrument; therefore, all is of the nature of Śiva.

rows.grounds: indeed properly established; fused form marked by +

items.question: Is the conclusion that all is of Śiva's nature reasonably and firmly established?
premises: The preceding argument removed instrumental limitations.
The ultimate ground was shown to pervade all.
A reasoned conclusion follows from this.
items.inference: Therefore, it is reasonable and indeed established that all is of the nature of Śiva.
items.plain_english: Therefore, it is reasonable and well established that all is indeed of the nature of Śiva. Thus, auspiciousness.

rows.grounds: in the commentary on the Śivadṛṣṭi

items.question: What textual section concludes with this colophon in the Śivadṛṣṭi commentary?
premises: The verse is a colophon formula.
It names the author and the work.
It specifies the chapter number.
items.inference: This marks the end of the second chapter in the commentary on the Śivadṛṣṭi.
items.plain_english: Thus ends the second chapter in the venerable commentary on the Śivadṛṣṭi composed by the revered Utpaladeva.

rows.grounds: the condition or level of śakti

items.question: Why is the state of power introduced after God has been revealed by reasoning?
premises: God has been revealed through reasoning.
The exposition now turns to the state of power.
A causal link is indicated for this transition.
items.inference: After God is revealed by reasoning, the state of power is introduced because it follows from that.
items.plain_english: God has been revealed by reasoning; thereafter the state of power is introduced, because—

rows.grounds: as the subject or agent, the state of being a person

items.question: How is establishment achieved through the standpoint of personhood in this context?
premises: The previous verse introduced the state of power.
Personhood provides a standpoint for explanation.
Establishment is sought through that standpoint.
items.inference: Establishment is made through personhood.
uncertainties: The verse is fragmentary in sense and depends on the following argument.
items.plain_english: —there is establishment through personhood.

rows.grounds: existing apart or excluded from Śiva

items.question: Can Śiva exist without power or power exist separately from Śiva?
premises: Śiva and śakti are being related.
If Śiva lacked śakti, he would be inert.
If śakti were separate, it would be independent of Śiva.
items.inference: Śiva is not devoid of power, and power is not separate from Śiva.
items.plain_english: Śiva is not without power, and power is not separate from him.

rows.grounds: of śakti and the possessor of śakti

items.question: Does Śaiva doctrine ever assert a real difference between power and the power-holder?
premises: Śiva and śakti have been declared inseparable.
Some views may posit difference between them.
The Śaiva position must be stated clearly.
items.inference: In the Śaiva doctrine, no difference between power and the power-holder is ever described.
items.plain_english: In the Śaiva teaching, no difference between power and the holder of power is ever asserted.

rows.grounds: in doctrines not accepted as authoritative

items.question: Where is a difference between power and power-holder wrongly asserted unlike in Śaivism?
premises: Śaivism denies difference between power and power-holder.
Other views may take a different position.
Those views are contrasted as unauthoritative.
items.inference: Such difference is asserted elsewhere, in unauthoritative views.
items.plain_english: As it is in other, unauthoritative views.

rows.grounds: an endless multiplication of names for that capacity

items.question: What problem arises if capacity is imagined as separate from the power-holder?
premises: One might posit capacity as distinct.
Distinct positing requires naming and delimiting it.
This leads to problematic consequences.
items.inference: If capacity were imagined separately, it would lead only to an endless proliferation of names.
uncertainties: The exact force of vā here may indicate an alternative formulation of the same fault.
items.plain_english: If capacity were imagined as separate, there would be only an endless multiplication of names for it.

rows.grounds: in the same way as Śiva
for the sake of functioning as an instrument or means

items.question: Would a separately posited power become a power-holder like Śiva for instrumental purposes?
premises: Capacity might be posited as separate for instrumental use.
To function instrumentally, it would need agency-like status.
That would make it analogous to Śiva as power-holder.
items.inference: The posited power would itself become a power-holder like Śiva for instrumental purposes.
items.plain_english: Then that power would itself become a power-holder, like Śiva, for the purpose of acting as an instrument.

rows.grounds: of one who lets go or emits
in the state of independence or autonomy

items.question: Would knowledge of freedom arise even when one is releasing one's own power?
premises: A power-holder may release or manifest power.
Freedom is intrinsic to the power-holder.
Knowledge of that freedom would still be present in the act.
items.inference: Even in releasing its own power, knowledge in freedom would occur.
uncertainties: The verse can be read as stating an entailment or as part of a reductio depending on context.
items.plain_english: Even when releasing its own power, knowledge would arise in freedom.

rows.grounds: of snow and fire as examples
the sensations of cold and heat

items.question: Are cold and heat perceived separately from snow and fire in ordinary experience?
premises: Snow and fire are associated with cold and heat.
The qualities are not experienced apart from their loci.
This analogy illustrates inseparability.
items.inference: Likewise, the cold and hot touches are not perceived separately from snow and fire.
items.plain_english: Likewise, the cold and hot touches are not perceived separately from snow and fire.

rows.grounds: in the state of being restrained or paralyzed by mantra
fire as the locus of heat

items.question: Why is fire not called fire in the same way when its heat is restrained by mantra?
premises: Fire is ordinarily identified with its heating power.
Mantra can restrain that manifest power.
The analogy supports inseparability of power and its locus.
items.inference: Indeed, when restrained by mantra, that is not then called fire in the usual sense.
uncertainties: The verse implies loss of the characteristic function rather than absolute nonexistence.
items.plain_english: Indeed, in the case of paralysis by mantra, that is not then called fire.
